items.title: LangSmith BYOC is now available on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud
items.summary: LangSmith BYOC now runs on AWS (GA), Azure and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, and agent deployments stay in your cloud account while LangChain runs it.
items.story_key: story|title:langsmith byoc is now available on aws azure and google cloud
items.content_excerpt: LangSmith Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) now runs on AWS (GA), Azure (Beta), and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, datasets, prompts, and agent deployments stay in your own cloud account, on the cloud you choose, and LangChain manages the data plane for you, from orchestration and scaling to platform updates. By splitting the control plane and data plane in two, BYOC provides greater flexibily to decide where agents run and where telemetry lives, without taking on the work of running LangSmith. LangChain runs the control plane , which holds auth, org and workspace config, billing metadata, hashed API keys, and static UI assets. You own the data plane , which holds everything sensitive, from traces, prompts, and datasets to experiments, agent deployments, and workspace secrets. An organization can hold several data planes, each in its specific account and region, and each data plane holds its workspaces. This lets you split data planes by region, environment, or business unit. For example, a platform team might run production and staging data planes in separate AWS accounts, while a business unit that standardized on Azure runs its own, separate BYOC deployment on Azure. Each team's traces land in the account that team owns. Until now, teams with strict compliance boundaries deployed and maintained self-hosted LangSmith. This kept their data inside their own boundary, but it took dedicated platform engineers to patch stateful services, configure databases, and run schema migrations. With BYOC, LangChain provisions and operates LangSmith inside your own virtual network. Consider a team running agent applications across several environments. With self-hosted, every update to the execution components meant coordinating downtime and managing custom Helm rollouts in each environment. With BYOC, the data in your data plane stays in your VPC while LangChain handles scaling, schema updates, and runtime dependencies. While self-hosting continues to be a reliable deployment option for customers who require complete control, BYOC provides the best of both worlds for customers who need it. Since we launched BYOC on AWS in August, many teams have chosen to run LangSmith in their own cloud with BYOC. They point to three main benefits: By expanding LangSmith BYOC to Azure and Google Cloud, more teams can get access to this experience while choosing their preferred cloud vendor. items.title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents
items.summary: Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.

items.title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response
items.summary: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/GeoFaham.

items.title: HARP: Training-Free Dual-Profile Agentic Communication for LLM-Based Recommendation
items.summary: In LLM-based recommendation, memory acts as a user-level agent in a memory-augmented backbone. Yet users and items remain asymmetric: only the user is given a structured profile; it enters a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt; and it is frozen after warmup. We recast LLM-based recommendation as an agentic-communication process in four stages: BUILD a self-description, TRANSMIT it along the collaborative graph, UNDERSTAND the other side, and SYNC it from the next interaction. This formulation reveals three unresolved communication challenges: the item side never produces a comparable self-description (one-sided BUILD); profile-level signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt rather than retrieval, where they would not compete for context tokens (prompt-trapped UNDERSTAND); and the user's description is frozen after warmup with no principled update rule (absent SYNC). We instantiate the missing stages as HARP (Homophily-aware Agentic Recommendation via dual Profiles), a training-free, three-operator addition to a frozen LLM backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile (zero extra LLM calls), a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily H(phi_u, phi_i) consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the reranker prompt, and a single-pass reflective update realising in-context profile evolution without any gradient step. On four public benchmarks (Yelp, Books, MovieTV, Goodreads), HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%-24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations and a per-case attribution study show that the operators contribute complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source; we also report the trade-off introduced by the reflective pass. We formulate agentic communication and provide a training-free instantiation. Code is available at https://github.com/Jove-Zhen/HARP.

items.summary: Editing Qwen’s weights to reduce reasoning loops, DeepSeek’s super-agent prototype, and the GDPx benchmark.

items.content_excerpt: Keyword matches words; semantic matches meaning and exact titles or names; hybrid combines both. In keyword mode, use quotation marks for exact phrases. Author matches published credits. Year applies to posts; wiki entries have no author or publication year. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. Editing Qwen’s weights to reduce reasoning loops, DeepSeek’s super-agent prototype, and the GDPx benchmark. Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears : Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the world has now gone from 0 to 1 on this very new RSI capability…. which will immediately put to use

items.title: New context engineering challenges in late 2026
items.summary: LangChain CEO Harrison Chase shares insights into the biggest harness engineering challenges with the emergence of proactive agents.
items.story_key: story|title:new context engineering challenges in late 2026
items.content_excerpt: It feels like everyone is converging on the same agent architecture: an LLM, running in a loop, calling tools, running in a sandbox. Claude Code - perhaps the first high profile manifestation of this - came out over a year and a half ago. Deep Agents , our agent harness, launched over a year ago. This pattern has been building for a while. There’s nothing bad with that convergence per se, but it has led to a sentiment among some AI engineers that I’ve talked to recently that “all the hard problems are solved” or “there’s no new AI engineering problems to solve”. When people express this sentiment, I think they are largely talking about the context engineering practices we do to make agents work. And to some extent they are right - there are a lot of standard-ish context engineering solutions we’ve all arrived at: The good news (for context engineering aficionados like myself) is that I think we’re seeing a step function change in agent capabilities, or at least how they are being used. Specifically, over the past few months every agent builder I’ve chatted with has been thinking about proactive, always on, goal-oriented agents . The core of this agent shares a lot of similarities with coding agents, but there are a set of new challenges as well. I highlight a few below. We (at LangChain, and in the industry) don’t necessarily have solutions (or at least, general solutions) for these, so thinking about these has been the most fun I’ve had in a while! How to be proactive without being annoying : These proactive agents run in the background and either listen to event feeds or are woken up with heartbeats. On one hand, they need to be able to push things to the user - that creates a sense of helping. On the other hand, if you push too many notifications to the user, you risk overwhelming them. Calibrating this to be a delightful experience (not too much, not too little) is still a hard context engineering challenge! Memory : Memory for agents has been something we’ve talked with builders about for a while. Memory systems end up having two parts: the underlying data structure and an intelligence layer (agent) around the data. The data structures are often pretty simple ( files , a single string). The hardest part of the intelligence layer is figuring out what to remember. items.title: What Is This Memory Useful For? Measuring Task-Conditioned Utility in Long-Term Agent Memory
items.summary:
A stored experience may answer one future question and offer little help with another. We measure this task-conditioned utility rather than assigning each memory a single importance score. A task-blind writer stores a memory without seeing the later task; a frozen reader then answers that task with and without the memory, using identical filler. A cost ledger records the resources used to form, store and expose the memory.
  On single-call factual-recall tasks built from LongMemEval-V2 web-agent memories, the same memory helps more when it contains information needed for the answer. Its mean paired reward gain on these answer-bearing task pairs exceeds that on matched-control pairs by $+0.33$ (95% interval $+0.21$ to $+0.46$). The tested task-blind summaries and structured records yield smaller gains than Raw, including at fixed total context; a budget sweep is consistent with retention of answer-bearing content contributing to the difference. The bearing--control contrast remains positive in a new session with randomized memory position and under a second reader, although individual memory--task labels change. Generic retrieval performs above chance but misses most screen-defined answer-bearing memories. The factual-recall gains do not extend to the tested software-engineering and scientific-coding benchmarks, where even raw memories have no measurable effect. We provide a public, versioned Conditional Memory Utility Dataset of paired measurements and costs. The practical takeaway is to evaluate memory compression by the task utility it preserves alongside its costs. Task-conditioned measurements make this comparison possible; their stability must also be checked.

items.title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
items.summary: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{LoopVQ}$, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.317
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a warning to /schedule when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
  • Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
  • Added onFailure: "block" for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run
  • Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do
  • Added a notice when auto mode's check has no answer for a subagent's tool call, which used to leave nothing in the main view
  • Added anthropic.plan, anthropic.seat_type, anthropic.provider and anthropic.custom_base_url to OTel metrics, events and spans
  • Added a cost report to the Claude apps gateway admin API, GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost, for reading past spend over a date range in total, per developer, per day or per IdP group
  • Added a daily record of each developer's IdP groups on Claude apps gateways with admin: set, kept for admin.identity_retention_days, which the cost report groups by
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NESTED_SESSION_ID: set it to 1 on a self-hosted runner to have claude -p run inside a session use that session's ID and transcript, as in earlier versions
  • Fixed project and local MCP servers disconnecting after the first turn in some Claude desktop sessions
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn when an LLM gateway set as the base URL answers 403 or 422 to its server-side safety check (a 403 with an apiKeyHelper is unchanged)
  • Fixed claude auth status exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed a project's effortLevel setting being ignored by sessions that an app starts ahead of time and then opens in the project, such as new sessions in the desktop app's Code tab
  • Fixed claude --from-pr reporting "No conversations found" in projects with many sessions when the linked session was older than the first page
  • Fixed the second of two simultaneous permission prompts showing no file path or command on claude.ai and the mobile apps
  • Fixed Remote Control and SDK hosts offering "don't ask again" on a mod's tool calls
  • Fixed session titles being lost in cloud and SDK sessions when a new message or Stop arrived while the title was generating
  • Fixed self-paced /loop wakeups sometimes not being scheduled when Claude left a field out of its request
  • Fixed auto mode in cloud sessions stopping for approval when the Artifact tool uploaded, wrote to a database or saved a file through the outputs folder
  • Fixed skills synced from claude.ai being lost or downloaded again every ten minutes when they can't be written to disk
  • Fixed /schedule leaving a cloud scheduled task's next run time and link out of its results after creating or updating it
  • Fixed screen readers speaking a running subagent's elapsed time and token count on every change in screen reader mode
  • Fixed a region or network block (HTTP 403) being shown as a sign-in failure; the error now explains the block
  • Fixed Claude saying a working claude.ai connector needed authorization or had failed in cloud sessions when a synced plugin included the same server
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 when a full disk or quota lost its transcript or ~/.claude.json writes; it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1. Full NFS exports may be missed
  • Fixed edits to settings files made in the first second or so after launch not taking effect until a settings file changed again
  • Fixed old transcripts not being cleaned up on machines where some runs skip cleanup, such as runs using --setting-sources
  • Fixed deleted agent team inboxes being re-created by a teammate's late message
  • Fixed a re-created agent teammate being removed from its team by an earlier shutdown approval
  • Fixed stored scheduled tasks being impossible to list or delete after scheduled tasks were turned off
  • Fixed Claude deleting your most recently updated /team-onboarding guide when asked to delete one without naming which
  • Fixed Claude saying a /team-onboarding guide was deleted when the server refused the delete
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway hiding Amazon Bedrock's "Input is too long." error, which left sessions failing every turn with "upstream rejected the request" instead of compacting
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions losing recent turns or the whole conversation when restarted while a plan waited for approval
  • Fixed "Prompt is too long" after automatic compaction in sessions whose very large CLAUDE.md changed since it was last sent
  • Fixed high memory use and slow startup in headless sessions with many plugins that register commands
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers receiving an empty AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK when their env config sets it to empty; the variable is now unset, so the server can use the machine's own AWS credentials
  • Fixed API requests failing with "unable to get local issuer certificate" behind some TLS-inspecting proxies after a root certificate renewal
  • Fixed very long conversations losing their earlier summary when compaction had to shorten its own request
  • Fixed a PDF's own metadata being able to make Read and @-mentions under-count its pages
  • Fixed DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_OPUS and DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_SONNET having no effect on [1m], other-region and undated spellings of the default model
  • Fixed /artifacts and the Artifact tool's shared list showing no shared artifacts when you have 200 or more of your own
  • Fixed Claude treating partial Grep and Glob results as complete when a search hit its time limit
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports to an https:// endpoint through a proxy never being sent when they started while another export was still in progress
  • Fixed a flood of connection attempts to a proxy that blocks (HTTP 403) OpenTelemetry exports to an http:// endpoint
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports hanging indefinitely behind a proxy that never answers; they now time out after 10 seconds, or OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT up to 30 seconds
  • Fixed resumed sessions telling Claude again about a file change it already knew about
  • Fixed Claude sometimes not using a built-in tool in a resumed session after an earlier call failed because the tool was switched off
  • Fixed /remote-control answering "Unknown command" instead of saying that Remote Control is turned off by the disableRemoteControl setting
  • Fixed agent team teammates in tmux or iTerm2 panes starting in auto mode when the lead session was in manual mode
  • Fixed a background session sometimes losing a just-made change of permission mode when it was upgraded or retired
  • Fixed Ctrl+C stopping all running background agents when pressed to clear typed text at the prompt
  • Fixed /feedback showing "Enter to confirm" while a report is being sent
  • Fixed child processes of a stopped shell command sometimes being sent SIGTERM twice, which could make some programs skip their cleanup
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session sharing that session's ID: it wrote into the session's transcript, and a restart could resume the wrong conversation
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session generating a title of its own and sending it to that session
  • Improved the error shown on Microsoft Foundry when Azure credentials can't be loaded: it now says to check or refresh them, and reports as cloud_credential_error
  • Improved /design-sync to say up front when your design system has moved to Claude, and stop before building instead of failing at upload
  • Improved the startup error when a required Claude apps gateway can't be reached: it points to the network instead of a sign-in, and says when the gateway's TLS certificate can't be verified
  • Improved the "Resume this session with" hint shown at exit to repeat the flags you launched with (for example --chrome --debug) ahead of --resume
  • Improved how self-hosted runners recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a runner's next poll now opens a new connection instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a session now opens new connections instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover when connections stop answering: after a heartbeat gets no answer, a session now opens new connections instead of trying each idle one in turn
  • Changed SendMessage so a message to a running background agent arrives earlier: its running command moves to the background, without being stopped
  • Changed subagents and teammates on a different model from the main conversation to use that model's saved effort level or its default, instead of the session's effort level
  • Changed exit to skip the "Background work is running" prompt for plugin monitors
  • Changed the built-in plugin-authoring skill to offer once, after a mod you built works, to help share the mod
  • Removed the Read tool's "file unchanged since your last Read" stub: reading an unchanged file again returns its content
  • Windows: Fixed every tool call being refused on some volumes where the native path lookup fails; the working-directory check now compares the folder's identity instead
  • Windows: Fixed the session scratchpad and other temporary paths growing with your project's path length in sessions not started by Claude Desktop, which made repositories cloned into them hit the 260-character path limit
  • Gateway: Fixed the status line and /usage showing a developer's own spend limit as 100% used after their group's pooled budget ran out
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed Claude not seeing the interrupted tool call when a session moves to a new runner and the turn is older than CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN_MAX_AGE_MS
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an MCP server that was switched off coming back on after the session moved to a new machine, when the session service had refused to save the switch
  • Remote Control: Improved fork names when the app doesn't set one: a long name keeps its "(fork)" ending, and in sessions started with claude remote-control a fork of "Name (fork)" is "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed forked conversations dropping messages: only one of the tool calls Claude ran in parallel was kept, and the last messages a compaction kept were lost, which could leave Claude's answer without the question it answered
  • [VSCode] Fixed a message being lost when Claude did not finish starting in time: the extension now starts Claude once more before showing the error
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen opening when a request is blocked for its region or network
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Account panel showing the plan name with a lower-cased second word
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links in a Claude tab opening on top of the chat instead of in another editor group
  • [VSCode] Fixed attachment chips, menus, banners and dialogs in the Claude panel staying small when chat.fontSize is raised
  • [VSCode] Fixed ultrathink not raising effort for its turn or showing its rainbow when telemetry is off
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a link card to cloud sessions, so you can open or decline a link an MCP server asks you to visit instead of the request going unseen
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the organization environment dialog in admin settings to the personal dialogs' short layout: each section opens from a row, and unsaved input asks before closing
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed adding a network secret for a host that already has one silently replacing it; the Add secret form now refuses and points you to the existing secret
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed new scheduled tasks ignoring your organization's default environment: the form now starts on the one an admin chose instead of the Anthropic-hosted default
  • [Remote Control] Fixed the next message to an idle session going unanswered after you restart claude remote-control, when you sent it within a minute of your previous message
  • [Claude Tag] Changed newly pasted artifact links in Slack to show a simpler card with an Open button that opens the artifact in Claude, instead of Slack's side panel

items.title: claude-agent-sdk-python v0.2.177
items.summary:
New Features

  • on_failure option for HookMatcher: Control what happens when a hook callback fails. Set on_failure="block" to block the action when a callback raises, returns None, or returns a value the CLI rejects. Defaults to "continue" (treat failure as no decision). Requires a CLI version that supports this option; connecting to an older CLI with on_failure="block" raises CLIConnectionError (#1460)

Internal/Other Changes

  • Updated bundled Claude CLI to version 2.1.317
  • Tests: e2e tests now accept either Bash or PowerShell tool in shell-dependent tests, fixing intermittent failures on Windows (#1467)

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/claude-agent-sdk/0.2.177/

items.title: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
items.summary: Genie 4: our new world model unlocking unprecedented realism in real-time simulation.
items.story_key: story|title:genie 4 a new generation of world simulation
items.content_excerpt: Today, we are announcing Genie 4, our new world model, which unlocks unprecedented realism and improves real-time interactive simulation. Genie 4 is natively multimodal, enabling audio-like music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue to be simultaneously generated with the world. The Genie 4 model incorporates and builds on capabilities from the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models provide the complex reasoning needed to help maintain a simulation’s coherence and continuity. With this foundation, you can set an event in motion, and Genie 4 simulates what happens next: how the world responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak. Understanding and simulating the world is a crucial aspect of building AGI. Genie 4 advances our ability to create safe, infinitely variable simulations that can help with everything from developing training environments for robots and agents to unlocking the creation of new interactive experiences. We have started rolling Genie 4 out as a research preview for trusted testers — gathering feedback before we release it to consumers and developers, starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie here . Genie 4 delivers enhanced photorealism, fluid movement, and native audio. All accompanying sounds featured above are produced directly by Genie 4. The following are recordings of real-time interactions from Genie 4, where users use standard keyboard controls for navigation and camera control, and text prompts to steer the scene as it evolves. With Genie 4, you can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time — like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object — and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene. Between your inputs, Gemini also monitors and steers the scene to keep the world progressing cohesively. Prompt: Use the reference image as the exact first frame and visual basis for the scene. Preserve the same floating rectangular platform, weathered concrete edges, wild grasses, ferns, twisted small tree, warm glowing amber sphere, and the same middle-aged man in a loose brown suit playing a brass saxophone.
